units.text: 09. How new rules arise without a new legislator

Imagine inhabitants of a universe containing only a large network of locally interacting elements. They discover persistent objects, waves, boundaries between regions and abrupt transitions. One declares: every new phenomenon proves that the world’s author added a rule. Another asks: might the same rule, repeated over many components, produce all this?

The second possibility is real in mathematical models. Cellular automata update cell states through local rules. Some systems with extremely simple descriptions have rich behavior. Matthew Cook proved the computational universality of Rule 110 in suitable configurations. The result concerns a formal system and its ability to simulate computation; it does not prove that our universe is a cellular automaton or that an arbitrarily chosen initial state will generate civilizations (Cook, 2004) .

It does not follow that every complexity comes from a short program. A two-line program replaying a gigantic file does not explain the file’s information. Rule simplicity must be evaluated together with the simplicity of the initial state and boundary conditions.

Consider a more modest model: on an unbounded line, independent particles take equal steps left or right with equal probabilities. There is no individual instruction to ‘spread out the concentration’. Yet the collective distribution has calculable properties.

If each step has length a, mean displacement is zero and mean squared displacement after n steps is n·a². Independence and equal probability are premises, not discoveries about every particle. The calculation follows because cross-correlation terms between steps average to zero. The characteristic distance thus grows as the square root of the number of steps. We have obtained a collective regularity without a coordinator tracking the entire cloud.

In appropriate limits, such models lead to diffusion descriptions. The point is not to identify every real molecule with a game coin, but to see the explanation’s form: specify the microscopic mechanism, choose collective variables, justify approximations and derive a relationship at another scale. ‘Emergence’ becomes informative only when we can show such transitions.

Sometimes multiple microscopic mechanisms lead to similar macroscopic behaviors. This is the idea of universality in precise contexts. Details differing between systems may become unimportant for certain quantities at certain scales. The renormalization group provides a framework for studying how descriptions transform when scale changes and for separating relevant details from those that matter increasingly less (Burgess, 2007) .

Coarse-graining represents multiple fine states at a common level; it does not physically erase details. Sometimes their effects are suppressed in the observables tracked; at other times ignored information returns and the model fails. The justification depends on the system.

This relative autonomy of levels explains why we can do science without knowing the ultimate basis. An inhabitant of a simulated world could discover correct fluid laws without knowing the processor. We can describe a material through collective variables without tracking each constituent. Being effective does not mean being fictional. It means being true or useful at a specified resolution and under specified conditions.

At least two meanings of emergence must nevertheless be distinguished. In the weak sense, collective behavior depends on components and rules but is difficult to anticipate or requires a new description. In the strong sense, properties or powers arise that would not, in principle, be determined or explainable by the complete basis according to the adopted criterion. The second meaning is a far more demanding thesis. Complexity and our surprise alone do not prove it.

Saying water ‘invents’ liquidity can be a good metaphor but does not replace analysis. First we must establish what we call a property, what ‘derivable’ means and what information about the basis we have allowed. Sometimes we cannot calculate. Sometimes we lack suitable concepts. At other times we claim ontological independence. These problems must not be crammed into one word.

Can new regularities arise without new fundamental rules? Yes, and models show us how. Emergence does not automatically explain why basic rules, an initial state or something rather than nothing exists. Demanding all these answers would turn explanation into a magic word.
